notes.title: Chain-of-Thought — Asking for the Working Before the Answer
notes.html:
References

Wei et al. 2022: chain-of-thought prompting · Kojima et al. 2022: zero-shot reasoners · Sprague et al. 2024: To CoT or not to CoT? · Anthropic: prompting best practices · OpenAI: reasoning best practices

TL;DR

Chain-of-thought asks the model to write out its steps before it commits to an answer, either by showing worked examples or with one added sentence. The steps go into the context, so each later token can read them. You pay for every one in output tokens and waiting time. The gain concentrates on maths and symbolic work. A model with built-in thinking now does this without being asked, so the prompted form is a fallback.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:question"work through it, then answer"model writes the stepseach step stays in the contextfinal answer in a tagcode reads the tag onlycount a failure

Recall

Prompt Answer
Few-shot vs zero-shot CoT? Worked examples in the prompt, or one trigger sentence and no examples.
Where do the gains concentrate? Maths, symbolic and logic tasks; about zero elsewhere (2024 meta-analysis).
Why tag the final answer? The working is full of numbers; code must find the one that counts.
Is the reasoning requested or enforced? Requested. Only the extractor and the token cap are enforced.
Does a reasoning model still need it? No. It is redundant there, and on some models visible working may be declined.
Draw by hand: the anatomy block Task with the trigger, constraints, optional worked examples, tagged context, output tag.

The idea

You ask: "Invoice total 4,800 includes 20% VAT. The late fee is 1.5% of the net amount per month. Two months late. What is owed? Reply with the number only." The first token has to be the answer. Nothing has yet produced the net amount, 4,000, or the fee of 60 a month, so the model is pattern-matching on numbers it can see, and the failure is a confident figure with no derivation behind it.

Change one line: "Work through the steps, then give the final figure in <answer> tags." Now the reply carries 4,000, then 60, then 120, then 4,920, and each is on the page when the next one is written. Why that helps has its own note. It is more specific than "the model gets more compute".

The instruction is a request. Nothing makes the steps correct, and a wrong first step gets built on.

The trade: you buy a chance at the multi-step answer and pay in output tokens, in latency before the answer, and in a parser that has to find the answer inside the working.

How it works

The engineered prompt, with the regions it needs.

① TASK         Work through the steps, then state the amount owed.          ← the trigger sits here
② CONSTRAINTS  Use only the figures given. If one is missing, name it.      ← a way out
③ EXAMPLES     <example>problem, worked steps, <answer>…</answer></example> ← few-shot form only
④ CONTEXT      <invoice>{{invoice_text}}</invoice>                          ← arrived text: data
⑤ OUTPUT       Put the final figure alone in <answer> tags.                 ← the one line code reads

Drop region ③ and it is zero-shot CoT; keep it and it is few-shot. Region ⑤ does the engineering.

Rule What actually happens
Working comes first A chain written after the answer can't change it. Order is the mechanism.
Few-shot sets the style Examples show how much working and in what form; the model follows that shape.
Zero-shot often used two calls Kojima's method extracts the answer in a second call. A tag does that job in one.
Cap the output Length is otherwise unbounded. A capped reply may have no tag, and that must count as a failure.
A step can be a tool's Arithmetic written by the model beats no working; a calculator beats both. Sprague: a solver outperformed CoT on the tasks it helps.

Evolution

Lineage:Jan 2022 few-shot CoTMay 2022 one sentence does it (zero-shot)May 2023 the chain shown not to be a faithful accountSep 2024 o1 moves reasoning inside the model; a meta-analysis scopes the gains2026 visible working may be declined on some models
  • Maturity: ⚪ Fading (Oct 2026) as a prompted technique. Anthropic's guide calls manual CoT "a fallback" for when thinking is off; OpenAI's says asking reasoning models to think step by step is "unnecessary". Replacement: the provider's thinking controls.
  • Stronger-model test: yes, for the trigger sentence. What won't change: a final answer your code can find, and the fact that the output tokens are paid for.
  • Checked on: the gains are from models of 2022 (Numbers). Vendor rows are in the chapter map's Landscape.

Code

The direct prompt against the working-first prompt.

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) What is owed? Reply with the number only. regions ① and ⑤
On the input the invoice above a figure with no derivation steps, then a tagged figure
Fails as commits at the first token —
The one edit — ① moving the answer after the working

Break it: the belief that any parser can read a reply with working in it.

import re
chain = "Net = 4800 / 1.2 = 4000. Fee = 1.5% of 4000 = 60 a month. Two months = 120.\n<answer>4920</answer>"
cut = "Net = 4800 / 1.2 = 4000. Fee = 1.5% of 4000"              # scripted: stopped at the token cap
first_number = lambda t: re.search(r"[\d.]+", t).group()
def tagged(t):
    m = re.search(r"<answer>(.*?)</answer>", t)
    return m.group(1) if m else None                             # None: count it, don't guess
print(first_number(chain), tagged(chain))
print(first_number(cut), tagged(cut))
# look for: the naive parser returns 4800 both times; the tag returns 4920, then None
# naive belief predicts: both parsers agree, and a cut-off reply still gives an answer

Run on Python 3.15, it prints 4800 4920 then 4800 None. The naive parser gives a wrong number twice and never reports a problem. The tag turns a truncation into a failure you can count.

Measure it

  • Offline: exact match on a golden set, sliced into tasks that need working and tasks that don't, against the direct prompt. Better means the first slice rises and the second doesn't fall.
  • In production: reasoning-to-answer token ratio per slice, the rate of replies with no tag, and refusals by category. A rising ratio on easy traffic means the route is leaking.
  • Enforced by: the extractor and the token cap, for shape and spend. That the steps are correct is a request only.

Interview

30-second answer: Chain-of-thought gets the model to write intermediate steps before the answer, with worked examples or one sentence. Steps stay in the context, so later tokens read them. Gains concentrate on maths and symbolic tasks and are near zero elsewhere. The gotcha is that I'd no longer prompt it on a model with built-in thinking; there I set effort and read a clean answer.

Q · Mechanism — Few-shot or zero-shot: what is the real difference? The trigger sentence asks for working; examples also define it. Few-shot is in-context learning over worked solutions, so the model copies the depth, the notation and the form of the steps. That's worth the input tokens when the style of working matters, such as a house method for a tax calculation. Zero-shot costs one sentence and leaves the form to the model. Kojima measured wording effects on one 2022 model, so a trigger phrase is a tuned parameter, not a law.

Q · Trade-off — Should CoT be on by default? No. The simpler rungs are a clearer instruction, examples and an output contract, and only a measured failure on a multi-step slice justifies the climb. Reasoning tokens are output tokens, written serially before the answer, and the gains are narrow. So I route it: on for the slice that needs derivation, off for classification and extraction. On a model that thinks by itself the question becomes which effort level to run.

Q · Failure — After adding CoT, accuracy is flat and the parse-failure rate jumps. The model now narrates, and the parser is reading the working. I'd confirm by sampling failures: the number extracted is an intermediate, or the reply has no tag because the cap cut it. The fix is a tagged final answer, a raised cap, and a count of replies with no tag. If accuracy really is flat, the slice didn't need reasoning, so I'd remove CoT rather than repair it.

Q · Design — A document-review service must justify every decision to an auditor. The binding constraint is that a chain is not a record of why. So the output is a verdict, citations to spans and a rule id from a versioned policy, all checkable by code: spans exist, the rule is valid. A second call, given only those, judges whether the evidence supports the verdict. Reasoning text stays a labelled debug artifact. I'd watch the citation-validity rate first. The prompt layer around this is the reference architecture.

Compare

Variant What you add Paid in Use when
Zero-shot CoT one sentence output tokens no thinking available, unknown task shape
Few-shot CoT worked examples input and output tokens the form of the working matters
Provider thinking a setting, not a prompt line thinking tokens, often hidden the model supports it

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Few-shot CoT gain 17.9 → 56.9% GSM8K, PaLM 540B, 8 exemplars, 2022 cited (paper): Wei et al.
Same, on Codex 19.7 → 63.1% GSM8K, code-davinci-002, 2022 cited (paper): Wei et al.
Zero-shot gain 17.7 → 78.7%; 10.4 → 40.7% MultiArith; GSM8K; text-davinci-002, 2022 cited (paper): Kojima et al.
Trigger wording 78.7% vs 57.5% "Let's think step by step" vs "Let's think", MultiArith, text-davinci-002 cited (paper): Kojima et al.

Scope and cost sit with their owner: when CoT hurts.

Pitfalls

  • "A longer chain means a better answer"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: long working looks careful, and hard problems do produce long chains.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: length tracks difficulty, not correctness. Every later step conditions on the earlier ones, so a wrong first step becomes a long, fluent, wrong derivation.
    ↳ Think instead: a chain raises the ceiling; only a check says whether this one reached it.
  • 🧙 Folklore: "Take a deep breath and work step by step"
    ↳ Why it spread: an optimiser found the phrase on PaLM 2 in 2023, and the screenshot travelled without its benchmark.
    ↳ What the evidence says: in the step-back paper it gave PaLM-2L 65.7% on MMLU Physics against 66.4% with nothing, and GPT-4 74.4% against 82.9% for plain CoT.
    ↳ Do instead: treat a trigger as a parameter and test it on your set.
  • Not the same: prompted CoT vs a reasoning model
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both produce steps before an answer, and vendors say "thinking" for the second.
    ↳ Difference: prompted CoT is a chat model imitating worked solutions; a reasoning model was trained on outcomes to run its own reasoning, usually hidden and governed by a setting.
    ↳ Think instead: ask whether the provider exposes a thinking control; if so, delete the trigger.
  • Don't ask for visible working on a model that thinks by itself.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: you want the steps for debugging, and the old prompt already has a <thinking> section.
    ↳ What goes wrong: Anthropic documents a billed reasoning_extraction refusal on its newest models for a scratchpad section or a reasoning JSON field (Oct 2026).
    ↳ Do instead: ask for a short explanation, and read summarised thinking from the API.
  • Don't switch CoT on for all traffic.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it is one sentence, so it looks free, and the eval set is often mostly hard cases.
    ↳ What goes wrong: easy traffic pays the same output tokens and waits behind the working, for no gain.
    ↳ Do instead: try the simpler rung first, and route by slice using the eval's bucket weights against live traffic.
  • Shelf life: the trigger sentence is already fading. A findable final answer and a bounded output are durable.

Connections

Path:in-context learningchain-of-thoughtwhy it worksself-consistencywhen it hurts
  • Builds on in-context learning: few-shot CoT uses the same mechanism over worked solutions.
  • Used by self-consistency: chains are the samples it votes over.
  • Owned elsewhere: output-format specification owns field order; chain-of-thought in an agent owns reasoning as a planning step.
  • Measured by golden datasets: the cohorts that expose a slice-level win.
  • Superseded by reasoning models: the same steps, produced without a prompt.
  • Drilled in reasoning model or prompted CoT.

notes.title: Why Chain-of-Thought Works — Written Steps, Not Extra Compute
notes.html:
References

Wei et al. 2022: chain-of-thought prompting · Sprague et al. 2024: To CoT or not to CoT? · Tam et al. 2024: Let Me Speak Freely? · Turpin et al. 2023: unfaithful explanations

TL;DR

The usual story is "more tokens, more compute". The paper that introduced the technique tested that and it failed: dots of the same length gave no gain. What helps is intermediate steps written in language or symbols, before the answer, which later tokens can read. So the working has to come first, it has to carry the partial results, and a wrong step stays in the context with the same standing as a right one.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:problemwrite step 1step 1 re-enters the contextstep 2 reads itpartial results pile upanswer conditioned on all of them

Recall

Prompt Answer
Did tokens alone help? No. Dots of equal length matched the baseline on GSM8K.
Did the chain after the answer help? No. It also matched the baseline: the steps must come first.
Which stage does CoT mostly help? Execution: computing and manipulating symbols, not planning.

The idea

You've heard the explanation: a transformer does a fixed amount of work per token, so 200 tokens buy 200 passes. That predicts any 200 tokens would do. Wei et al. ran that prediction: they prompted the model to output only dots, as many as the characters in the equation. It performed about as well as no CoT at all.

So tokens are necessary and not sufficient. Compare a reply that gives the answer and then explains: the reasoning exists, the tokens were spent, and the answer was already out. It matched the baseline too.

What's left is the combination: written partial results, ahead of the answer, that the next tokens condition on. The model doesn't need to hold 4,000 anywhere when 4,000 is in the context.

This is a request. Nothing guarantees that the partial results are right.

The trade: the steps do the work only if they are real intermediates, so the model has to spend output tokens on them before you see an answer.

How it works

Same model, same benchmark.

Only the written chain, ahead of the answer, moves the number. On GSM8K the equation alone doesn't either, because its questions need language to reach the equation; on one- or two-step benchmarks it does help.

Rule What actually happens
Compute alone: no Dots matched the baseline, so length without content buys nothing.
Knowledge recall alone: no A chain written after the answer didn't help. The answer has to depend on it.
The steps are read back A later step conditions on what is written, so 4,000 needn't be re-derived.
Execution, more than planning Sprague: CoT mainly helps the step that computes, and a real solver does that better.
It needs a large enough model In Wei's tests the smallest models got worse: GPT 350M fell from 2.2% to 0.5%.

Evolution

Lineage:Jan 2022 ablations rule out compute aloneMay 2023 reasoning shown to be unfaithful, yet usefulAug 2024 a strict format with the answer first removes the gainSep 2024 execution named as the part that helps
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): the result has stood since 2022 and is later echoed by format studies.
  • Stronger-model test: no. The mechanism doesn't age: a reasoning model does this in hidden tokens. What won't change: a step that isn't written can't be read by the next token.
  • Checked on: LaMDA 137B and PaLM 540B (2022) for the ablations. The dots result has not been re-run on a current model, as far as I found.

Code

What order does to the same request.

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) Give the amount owed, then explain how you got it. Work through the steps, then give the amount owed.
On the input the invoice from chain-of-thought the figure is fixed at the first token; the rest defends it each partial result is available when the figure is written
Fails as a justification after the fact —
The one edit — moving the answer after the working

The same thing happens through a schema. Tam et al. found that all of GPT-3.5 Turbo's JSON-mode replies on Last Letter put answer before reason, which made zero-shot CoT into direct answering. Output-format specification owns field order.

Measure it

  • Offline: on your multi-step slice, compare direct, answer-then-explain and working-first prompts. If working-first doesn't beat the other two, the task isn't using the steps.
  • In production: share of replies where the answer appears before the working, and of wrong answers traced to a dropped or miscopied intermediate.
  • Enforced by: a request only, for the content of the steps. Order can be enforced by an extractor that rejects an answer found ahead of the working.

Interview

30-second answer: Chain-of-thought works because written intermediate steps sit ahead of the answer and later tokens condition on them. It isn't just more compute: Wei et al. replaced the chain with dots of the same length and got no gain, and a chain after the answer didn't help either. Most of the benefit is in executing computation. So the gotcha is that a wrong written step is read back as trustworthy.

Q · Mechanism — If the reasoning needn't be faithful, why does its quality matter? They're different properties. Faithful means the text reports what really drove the answer, and Turpin shows it often doesn't. Quality means the intermediates are right. A written step is an input to the next, so a bad one is conditioned on, while an unmentioned bias can still steer the result. So I invest in the steps being correct, with worked examples or named fields, and invest nothing in reading them as an explanation.

Q · Trade-off — When doesn't this mechanism pay? The simpler rung is a direct prompt with an output contract, right when the answer doesn't depend on intermediate results: recall, most classification, tone. The mechanism explains how CoT can help, not whether it will on my task, and the evidence says the gains are narrow. If the work is pure arithmetic, I'd give the step to a tool: a solver beat CoT in Sprague's tests.

Pitfalls

  • "It works because each token is another forward pass"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's true of how tokens are generated, and it sounds rigorous in an interview.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it predicts that dots help. Wei tested dots on LaMDA 137B: 6.4% against a 6.5% baseline.
    ↳ Think instead: tokens are the cost; written intermediates are the mechanism.
  • "Its content doesn't matter, only that it's generated"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: unfaithful chains still raise accuracy, so the text looks incidental.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a chain with no real intermediates has nothing for later tokens to read. Unfaithful isn't the same as empty.
    ↳ Think instead: the steps have to compute something, even when they misreport why.
  • Not the same: faithful reasoning vs useful reasoning
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are judged by reading the same text, which looks like an explanation.
    ↳ Difference: useful means the steps raised accuracy; faithful means they report the real cause of the answer. A chain can be the first and not the second.
    ↳ Think instead: measure usefulness on an eval, and never infer faithfulness from it.
  • Don't turn the mechanism into a reason for longer chains.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: if steps help, more steps should help more.
    ↳ What goes wrong: past the steps the problem needs, extra text adds cost and places to go wrong, not intermediates.
    ↳ Do instead: a short chain with named partial results; if one step is arithmetic, use a tool, the simpler rung.
  • Shelf life: the ablations are about how text generation works, so they should last. How much a model needs written out changes as models improve.

Connections

Path:chain-of-thoughtwhy it workswhen it hurtsreasoning models
  • Builds on chain-of-thought: the technique this note explains.
  • Owned elsewhere: chain-of-thought (LLM-Production) covers the generation mechanics.
  • Contrasts with when CoT hurts: same steps, read as costs and as false explanations.
  • Used by self-consistency: wrong steps diverge, which is why voting helps.
  • Drilled in why CoT works.

notes.title: Self-Consistency — Sampling Many Chains and Voting on the Answers
notes.html:
References

Wang et al. 2022: self-consistency · Wei et al. 2022: chain-of-thought prompting · Huang et al. 2023: LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet · Snell et al. 2024: scaling test-time compute · Anthropic: API version 2026-10-21, sampling parameters

TL;DR

Self-consistency runs the same prompt N times, pulls out each final answer, and takes the one most samples agree on. Correct paths tend to converge; wrong ones tend to scatter. You pay N times the tokens and get two outputs: the winning answer and a vote share you can route on. A vote separates popular from unpopular, not right from wrong, so a shared mistake wins unanimously.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:one prompt3 parallel samplesextract each answernormalisevoteaccept
7 more samplesvoteacceptescalate

Recall

Prompt Answer
What do you vote on? The extracted final answer, never the reasoning text.
Hard prerequisite? An equivalence: answers must be comparable after normalising.
Why can it beat one sample at p below 0.5? Wrong answers split; the right one only has to beat the largest.
What does vote share give you? A routing signal: accept, escalate or send to a person.
What does it miss? A shared error: every sample agrees and all are wrong.
Draw by hand: the vote Curves against N: two answers p=0.6 rises; p=0.4 falls; scattered p=0.4 rises.

The idea

A contract says "net 45 from invoice date", dated 12 March. Greedy decoding gives you one path, and if that path counts the days inclusively you get 27 April, with nothing to show it was close. Ask five times and you might get 26, 26, 27, 26, 27. Now you have an answer and a measure of doubt.

That's the whole change: the prompt is the same; your code runs it N times, normalises the answers and counts. The paper's argument: the answer you want maximises the probability summed across reasoning paths, and N samples estimate that sum, while one greedy path doesn't.

You think agreement means correct. It doesn't. Five samples reading the same clause the same wrong way vote unanimously for the wrong date, and your router trusts that case most.

The vote itself is enforced by code. Whether the samples are right is not.

The trade: N times the tokens buys a better guess and a confidence signal, but only when answers can be compared and errors aren't shared.

How it works

This note owns the vote arithmetic for the pillar. With per-sample accuracy p and independent samples:

two answers possible: P(vote right) = Σ[k > N/2] C(N,k) · pᵏ · (1−p)ᴺ⁻ᵏ   ← binomial tail, N odd
p = 0.6 : N=1 0.60 · N=3 0.648 · N=9 0.733 · N=25 0.846                  ← the vote amplifies the leader
p = 0.4 : N=1 0.40 · N=3 0.352 · N=9 0.267 · N=25 0.154                  ← ...in either direction
wrong mass split over many answers: right answer needs only a plurality  ← why scatter matters
N → ∞ : a question is right if and only if the right answer is the mode  ← the ceiling

The third case is what makes the method work on hard questions.

Same p, opposite results: the shape of the wrong answers decides, and most of the movement is at small N.

Rule What actually happens
Samples must differ The paper used T = 0.5–0.7. At temperature 0 you pay N times for about one answer.
Normalise before counting Without an equivalence, "26 Apr" and "26 April" split the right answer.
Agreement tracks accuracy On GSM8K, the paper found consistency highly correlated with accuracy, so low share means "don't trust this".
Escalate in tiers Stop at 3 if unanimous; add samples only on a split. Cost is then a distribution, so cap N.
Independence is an assumption One model's samples share its blind spots, so real curves stop short of the formula.

Evolution

Lineage:Jan 2022 CoT, one greedy pathMar 2022 self-consistencyOct 2023 re-used as the fair baseline for debate between modelsAug 2024 test-time compute treats voting as one allocation2026 reasoning models hide the sampling knobs
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026). The vote is durable, while how you get diverse samples is moving: Anthropic's models from 4.7 on reject non-default temperature, and OpenAI says to remove it when reasoning effort isn't none.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. A reasoning model or a higher effort setting often buys the same gain more cheaply, so compare first. What won't change: N independent answers are a confidence signal one reply can't give.
  • Checked on: PaLM-540B and code-davinci-002 (2022). Default sampling still varies on current models, but I found no published vote gain on them.

Code

One sample against N samples. The prompt is unchanged; code does the rest.

① TASK         Work out the due date for this invoice, step by step.      ← chains to sample
② CONSTRAINTS  Count calendar days; the invoice date is day 0.            ← removes a shared error
③ CONTEXT      <terms>{{payment_terms}}</terms>                           ← arrived text: data
④ OUTPUT       Final line: <answer>YYYY-MM-DD</answer>                    ← the comparable form
🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) the prompt above, one call the same prompt, N calls, with region ④ normalised and counted
On the input "net 45", dated 12 March one date, no signal of doubt a date plus a vote share; a split is escalated
Fails as a single unlucky path —
The one edit — ④ a comparable answer: without it there is nothing to count

Break it: the belief that voting finds the right answer on its own, and that a full vote proves it.

from collections import Counter
def vote(xs):
    (a, n), = Counter(xs).most_common(1)
    return a, n / len(xs)                                        # answer, vote share
canon = lambda s: s[:6]                                          # the equivalence: day + month
raw = ["26 Apr", "26 April", "27 Apr", "27 Apr", "26 Apr 2026"]  # scripted samples; 26 Apr is right
print(vote(raw))
print(vote([canon(x) for x in raw]))
print(vote(["27 Apr"] * 5))                                      # one shared wrong reading
# look for: raw strings elect the wrong date; canon fixes it; unanimity on a wrong answer scores 1.0
# naive belief predicts: 26 Apr all three times, and share 1.0 means correct

Run on Python 3.15, it prints ('27 Apr', 0.4), ('26 Apr', 0.6), ('27 Apr', 1.0). A majority of samples was right in the raw list, and the unnormalised vote still chose wrong.

Measure it

  • Offline: accuracy at N = 1, 3, 5 and 10 on a golden set, against one sample on the same model. Also accuracy within each vote-share band: higher share must mean higher accuracy.
  • In production: vote-share distribution, escalation rate and samples per request. An audit sample of unanimous accepts catches the shared error nothing else sees.
  • Enforced by: the vote and the routing rule, which are your code. Correctness isn't enforced: add a deterministic check on the accepted value.

Interview

30-second answer: Self-consistency samples N chains, extracts each answer and takes the majority. Correct paths tend to converge and wrong ones scatter, so the mode beats a single draw. It costs N times the tokens, needs comparable answers, and gives a vote share I can route on. The gotcha: agreement isn't correctness, so a shared error wins unanimously, and I audit-sample those.

Q · Mechanism — Why does voting beat one greedy chain? Greedy decoding follows one path. The answer you want is the one with most probability summed over all paths, and many low-probability paths can land on it. Sampling estimates that sum. The asymmetry comes from errors: there are many ways to be wrong and they land on different answers, so a right answer at p = 0.4 can still win. If the wrong answers bunch on one value, the same vote gets worse with N.

Q · Trade-off — Is it worth N times the tokens? The simpler rung is a verifier. If code can check the answer, generate and check, because a check separates right from popular and a vote can't. Next is one call on a stronger model or at higher effort. I'd add voting when no check exists and answers are comparable, and mostly for the confidence signal. Parallel calls keep wall-clock near one call, so the money is the real cost. Most of the gain arrives at small N, so sweep it.

Q · Failure — The audit finds wrong answers among unanimous, auto-accepted extractions. Agreement was treated as truth. A systematic error makes every sample agree, which is exactly the case the router trusts. I'd confirm by grouping audited errors: they share a clause type, so it isn't noise. The fix goes where the error is: a constraint or example in the prompt, plus a deterministic check. The audit sample stays. A rise in unanimous errors after a model upgrade is the signal to re-calibrate.

Q · Design — Extract payment terms from contracts where a wrong value reaches billing. The binding constraint is asymmetric cost: a wrong term costs far more than a review. So the goal is calibrated abstention. Run 3 samples; unanimous goes to a deterministic check (parses, appears verbatim, in range), split escalates to 10, and anything still close goes to a person. Log the full vote. I'd watch unanimous-but-wrong in the audit sample first, then the escalation rate, which moves when documents or the model change. Budget it through cost modelling.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Vote over greedy CoT 56.5 → 74.4% GSM8K, PaLM-540B, 40 paths, 2022 cited (paper): Wang et al.
Same, on Codex 60.1 → 78.0% GSM8K, code-davinci-002, 40 paths, T = 0.7, 2022 cited (paper): Wang et al.
With small N 76.7 → 82.5% (N=3) → 85.3% (N=6) GSM8K, GPT-3.5, 2023; debate at 6 responses got 83.2% cited (paper): Huang et al.
Expected samples, tiers 3 then 10 3 + 7·(1−u); 4.4 at u = 0.8 u = share unanimous at 3, assumed derived
Token multiplier N × output tokens parallel: about 1× wall-clock derived

Pitfalls

  • "High agreement means the answer is right"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the paper reports that agreement correlates with accuracy, and five of five feels like proof.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: correlation across a dataset says nothing about a shared error on one case. The vote ignores what no sample got right.
    ↳ Think instead: agreement measures consistency; only a check or an audit measures correctness.
  • "You vote on the reasoning"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the chains are what you sampled, and they look like the work.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: diverse chains are the mechanism, so comparing them finds disagreement everywhere. Only final answers can be counted.
    ↳ Think instead: many routes, one comparable destination: count destinations.
  • Not the same: temperature for diversity vs temperature for determinism
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: teams set a low temperature for stable outputs, then add sampling on top.
    ↳ Difference: this method needs variation; deterministic prompting tries to remove it.
    ↳ Think instead: check that samples differ; if you can't set temperature, confirm the default gives enough variety before relying on a vote.
  • Don't vote where a verifier exists.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: voting needs no extra engineering beyond a loop.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you pay N times for popularity when a few lines of code could test the answer: parse it, find it in the document, run the test.
    ↳ Do instead: take the simpler rung, the check, first, and vote only on what can't be checked.
  • Don't vote on free text.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: summaries also benefit from a second opinion.
    ↳ What goes wrong: no two summaries match, so the vote has nothing to count, and clustering by embedding hides real differences.
    ↳ Do instead: vote on one comparable field, or use a judge with a rubric.
  • Shelf life: the arithmetic is permanent. Whether you can set sampling parameters, and whether a reasoning model makes N calls unnecessary, is provider-specific and moving.

Connections

Path:chain-of-thoughtself-consistencyself-refine loopsreasoning models
  • Builds on chain-of-thought: chains are the samples.
  • Contrasts with deterministic prompting: one needs varied samples, the other removes them.
  • Owned elsewhere: self-consistency and decomposition (LLM-Production) places it among test-time methods.
  • Measured by golden datasets: accuracy per vote-share band needs a labelled set.
  • Costed in cost modelling: N times the output tokens.
  • Drilled in self-consistency.

notes.title: Least-to-Most Prompting — Decompose, Then Solve in Order
notes.html:
References

Zhou et al. 2022: Least-to-Most Prompting

TL;DR

Least-to-most first breaks a problem into ordered sub-problems, then solves them one at a time, each with the earlier answers in context. It fixed chain-of-thought's weak spot: examples of easy problems didn't carry over to harder ones. For the loop version, see task decomposition.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
The two stages Decompose into ordered sub-problems, then solve them in sequence.
What it fixed Easy-to-hard generalisation: SCAN length split, 16.2% with CoT to 99.7% on code-davinci-002 (2022).
Main failure A wrong decomposition: every later step solves the wrong sub-problem correctly.

The idea

With CoT, worked examples are short, so a longer problem has no pattern to copy. Least-to-most gets the shorter sub-problems out first, and each answer feeds the next. On last-letter concatenation of 12 words it reached 74.0% against CoT's 31.8%, same model, same year.

The cost is an extra stage, and the first stage is itself a request that can go wrong. As a prompt pattern it's a chain; the gains are on short, uniform benchmarks, and reasoning models now decompose by themselves.

Evolution

Lineage:Jan 2022 CoTMay 2022 least-to-most2023 plan-first promptsSep 2024 reasoning models decompose internally. ⚪ Fading (Oct 2026). Replacement: reasoning models, or an explicit chain when you must inspect each step.

notes.title: Plan-and-Solve Prompting — Write the Plan, Then Follow It
notes.html:
References

Wang et al. 2023: Plan-and-Solve Prompting

TL;DR

Plan-and-solve is zero-shot chain-of-thought with a longer trigger: devise a plan, then carry it out step by step. It stays in one call and uses no examples. Its target is the step the model skips. As a separate plan in a loop, it's plan-and-execute.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
The move Replace "think step by step" with "devise a plan, then carry it out".
vs least-to-most One call, no sub-problem list, and no examples.
The size of the gain Modest: GSM8K 56.4% to 58.2%, text-davinci-003, 2023.

The idea

Zero-shot CoT sometimes leaves out a needed operation. Wang et al. listed the error types: missing steps made up 12% of 46 errors they examined. Asking for the plan first lists the steps before any is run.

① TASK    Understand the problem and devise a plan.         ← the plan first
② TASK    Then carry out the plan step by step.             ← the working second

The extended PS+ wording also asks it to extract variables and compute carefully: GSM8K 59.3%, and a six-dataset mean of 76.7% against CoT's 70.4%. A planning line is a request, so nothing checks the plan is followed.

Evolution

Lineage:May 2022 zero-shot CoTMay 2023 plan-and-solveSep 2024 reasoning models plan internally. ⚪ Fading (Oct 2026). Replacement: reasoning models: Anthropic's guide now prefers general instructions to prescribed steps.

notes.title: Step-Back Prompting — Name the Principle, Then Answer
notes.html:
References

Zheng et al. 2023: Take a Step Back · Wei et al. 2022: chain-of-thought prompting

TL;DR

Step-back asks a more general question first, recalls the principle behind it, then answers the original with that principle in view. It fits questions buried in specifics, where the failing part is recalling the right rule. It costs a second step, and it does little where the rule is already easy to reach. The use as a query rewrite for retrieval belongs to RAG.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:specific questionwrite the general questionstate the principlereason from itanswer the original

Recall

Prompt Answer
The two steps? Abstraction (the general question), then reasoning from what it recalls.
Where do most errors remain? At the reasoning step: over 90%, not the principle.
vs CoT? CoT goes forward through steps; step-back first goes up a level.

The idea

Ask "What happens to the pressure of an ideal gas if the temperature doubles and the volume rises eightfold?" and the model starts on the specifics: it has to pick the right law while juggling the numbers, and a slip at the start colours everything after. Plain CoT walks forward from that same place.

Step-back inserts one move first: "What physics principle applies here?" The reply names the ideal gas law, PV = nRT, and now the working starts from it. The general question is often easier to answer than the specific one, and its answer is a better context for the next step.

It's a request, in one call or two. Nothing checks that the principle is the right one, so it adds a place to be wrong and a place to look.

The trade: you spend tokens or a call on the abstraction for a better starting point, and only some questions need one.

How it works

The prompt, in one call. The paper's own form uses few-shot examples of the abstraction.

① TASK      First state the general principle behind the question.      ← the abstraction
② TASK      Then use that principle to answer the question.             ← the reasoning
③ EXAMPLES  <example>question, principle, answer</example>              ← shows what "general" means here
④ CONTEXT   <question>{{question}}</question>                           ← arrived text
⑤ OUTPUT    Principle in <principle> tags, final answer in <answer>.    ← both can be logged
Rule What actually happens
Examples set the level Too general is useless. The paper gives few-shot exemplars of the abstraction.
Abstraction was seldom the failure Over 90% of remaining errors were in reasoning; the principle itself rarely failed.
On retrieval, it broadens the search Step-back plus RAG: TimeQA 68.7% against 57.4% for RAG alone, on PaLM-2L.
The gain shrinks as models improve On GPT-4 the edge over CoT was small; see Numbers.

Evolution

Lineage:2022 CoT moves forward from specificsOct 2023 step-back adds abstraction firstlater adopted as a RAG query transform2026 still a useful pattern in retrieval; redundant inside a reasoning model
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026) as a query transform; its use in reasoning alone is fading.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. It fades as a reasoning prompt. What won't change: a general query can retrieve what a specific one misses.
  • Checked on: PaLM-2L, GPT-4 and Llama2-70B, 2023.

Code

The direct prompt against step-back, on the question above.

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) Think step by step, then answer. ① and ②: State the principle, then use it.
On the input the gas question starts in the numbers starts from PV = nRT
Fails as the wrong rule chosen in passing —
The one edit — ① one general question ahead of the working

Measure it

  • Offline: accuracy against plain CoT on a set where the specifics distract; also how many logged principles a reviewer marks correct.
  • In production: share of wrong answers with a wrong principle against a wrong step; retrieval recall, if it's used in RAG.
  • Enforced by: a request only, for the principle. The tags can be checked by code; the correctness can't.

Interview

30-second answer: Step-back makes the model ask a general question and recall the principle before it answers, so the reasoning starts from the rule, not the specifics. It helped PaLM-2L a lot on physics, chemistry and time questions. The gotcha is that on GPT-4 it barely beat CoT, and most errors stayed in reasoning, so I'd use it mainly as a retrieval transform.

Q · Mechanism — Why would a more general question help? It's usually easier to answer and has more ways to be right, so it adds a correct fact to the context before the hard part. For retrieval, the same move adds a broader query that finds background a narrow one misses, which is why TimeQA gained. In the paper, the steps after the abstraction still produced over 90% of the errors, so it fixes the start of the path.

Q · Trade-off — Would you use it on a reasoning model? Not as a prompt. The simpler rung is plain instruction, and such a model usually picks its own abstractions, so an extra step adds tokens and may conflict with its plan. For retrieval I'd still test it, since the model doesn't see what the search didn't return. There it competes with sub-question decomposition, which goes the other way, into narrower parts.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Science gain 66.4 → 73.2; 70.9 → 81.8% MMLU Physics; Chemistry; PaLM-2L, 2023 cited (paper): Zheng et al.
Knowledge gain 41.5 → 68.7% TimeQA, step-back + RAG, PaLM-2L cited (paper): Zheng et al.
Over CoT on GPT-4 82.9 → 84.5; 85.3 → 85.6% MMLU Physics; Chemistry cited (paper): Zheng et al.

Pitfalls

  • "Abstraction is where these models fail"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the technique's story is about finding the right principle.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: in the paper's error analysis, reasoning produced over 90% of the remaining errors and the principle very few.
    ↳ Think instead: it improves the start of a path that can still go wrong.
  • Not the same: step-back vs decomposition
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both add a question before answering, and both appear as RAG transforms.
    ↳ Difference: step-back goes up to one broader question; decomposition goes down into several narrower ones.
    ↳ Think instead: background missing means step back; several hops means decompose.
  • Not the same: a PaLM-2L gain vs a gain today
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the headline numbers are big, and they're quoted with no model name.
    ↳ Difference: the large gains are on PaLM-2L. On GPT-4 with plain CoT as the baseline, the gain nearly vanishes.
    ↳ Think instead: quote benchmark, model and year, then re-test.
  • Don't add a step-back call to a prompt that already works.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's cheap to add, and a principle in the logs looks thorough.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a two-call version adds a round trip, and a poor principle can mislead the answer.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler rung is one clear prompt. Add the step for a slice that misses the rule.
  • Shelf life: as a reasoning prompt it is fading; as a retrieval transform it depends on your index, so test it there.

Connections

Path:chain-of-thoughtstep-backstep-back in RAG
  • Owned elsewhere: step-back in RAG owns the query-transform use.
  • Contrasts with least-to-most: goes down into sub-problems, not up to a principle.
  • Used by sub-question decomposition: the opposite transform, often tested alongside.
  • Superseded by reasoning models: for reasoning, not for retrieval.

notes.title: Tree of Thoughts & Graph of Thoughts — Search Over Partial Answers
notes.html:
References

Yao et al. 2023: Tree of Thoughts · Besta et al. 2023: Graph of Thoughts

TL;DR

Tree of Thoughts treats reasoning as search: propose several next steps, score them, follow the promising ones, and back up from dead ends. Graph of Thoughts also merges branches. The cost and the search loop are owned by tree of thoughts in Agentic; this note covers the prompting.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
The two prompts One proposes next steps; one scores partial states.
GoT adds Merging and reusing thoughts, not only branching.
The catch Needs a usable score to prune; calls multiply with breadth and depth.

The idea

A chain can't undo a bad first step. In Game of 24 on GPT-4, plain CoT solved 4% and ToT at breadth 5 solved 74%, while CoT with self-consistency solved 9%. ToT cost $0.74 per case against $0.47 for the best-of-100 CoT run (49%), at 2023 prices.

The gains are on puzzles with checkable partial states. GoT's sorting result, 62% better quality than ToT at over 31% lower cost, is on ChatGPT-3.5. The propose and score prompts are requests, so a confident wrong score prunes the right branch.

Evolution

Lineage:May 2023 Tree of ThoughtsAug 2023 Graph of ThoughtsSep 2024 reasoning models backtrack inside one call. ⚪ Fading (Oct 2026). Replacement: reasoning models; explicit search stays for small checkable state spaces.

notes.title: Self-Refine — Draft, Critique, Rewrite, and Keep the Best
notes.html:
References

Madaan et al. 2023: Self-Refine · Huang et al. 2023: LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning yet · Anthropic: prompting best practices

TL;DR

Self-refine runs a loop over one output: draft, critique it, rewrite using the critique, for a few rounds, in separate calls. It helps most when "better" has several dimensions, as with tone or coverage. Without an external signal it can lower accuracy on reasoning tasks, because the model can talk itself out of a right answer. So cap the rounds, keep the best draft (which isn't always the last), and score with something other than the same model where you can.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:draftcritique against criteriarewritescorebetter? keepround capbest draft out

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which tasks gain? Multi-criteria outputs: dialogue, tone, coverage. Far less on correct-or-wrong answers.
What is the risk without a signal? Self-critique changes right answers to wrong ones.
Why keep the best, not the last? Scores can fall during a round. The last draft isn't guaranteed best.

The idea

A reply to a customer comes out correct but stiff. You ask the same model to review it against three criteria and rewrite. The second version is warmer and covers the refund: a critique had something to find.

Now try the same loop on arithmetic. The answer is right. The critique prompt asks what is wrong, so it finds something, and the rewrite changes a right figure. Huang et al. tested this: with no outside signal, GPT-3.5 on CommonSenseQA fell from 75.8% to 38.1%. Given a correct-or-not signal from labels instead, GPT-3.5 on GSM8K rose from 75.9% to 84.3%. The critique was only as good as what fed it.

The criteria are a request. The cap on rounds and the kept best draft are enforced by your code.

The trade: you pay full calls per round for a better draft on subjective work, and take on a loop that can make it worse.

How it works

The loop runs in your code, each step a separate call.

Rule What actually happens
Critique against named criteria "Improve this" invites change for its own sake; a list gives it something to check.
The stop condition is yours The paper stops at a model-written stop line or four rounds. Your code holds the cap.
The signal decides A test, schema or label is outside the model. A self-score isn't.
Models can say all is well ChatGPT feedback said "everything looks good" on 94% of the math cases.
Rounds add up Derived, with one critique-and-rewrite call per round: 1 + 2 = 3 model calls for two rounds, plus scores.

Evolution

Lineage:Mar 2023 Self-RefineMar 2023 Reflexion carries lessons across attemptsOct 2023 self-correction shown to fail without a signal2026 Anthropic names self-correction the common chain, and adds a verify line
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): still used for writing, and now done by reasoning models inside one call for many tasks.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. Thinking covers some of it within a call. What won't change: a critique needs a source of truth to improve accuracy.
  • Checked on: GPT-3.5, ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Llama-2, 2023.

Code

The critique prompt, before and after.

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) Review your answer and fix any mistakes. Check the draft against: covers refund, under 80 words, polite. Name failures, then rewrite.
On the input a correct reply invents a flaw, changes it named checks pass, so no change is needed
Fails as right answer overwritten —
The one edit — naming the checks, so that "no change" is a possible outcome

Break it: the belief that the last round is the best.

drafts = [("v1", .62), ("v2", .71), ("v3", .66)]   # scripted scores, per round
last = drafts[-1]
best = max(drafts, key=lambda d: d[1])
print(last, best)
# look for: last is v3 at 0.66, best is v2 at 0.71
# naive belief predicts: the two are the same draft

Run on Python 3.15, it prints ('v3', 0.66) ('v2', 0.71). The scores are scripted; the selection line is the fix.

Measure it

  • Offline: score after each round on a golden set, against no loop. Look for the round where the mean stops rising, and how many right drafts turned wrong.
  • In production: rounds used, score change per round, and the share of finished outputs that aren't the last draft.
  • Enforced by: the code that holds the cap and the kept best. Whether a critique is honest is a request.

Interview

30-second answer: Self-refine loops draft, critique and rewrite over one output, in separate calls. On multi-criteria writing it gains a lot. On reasoning it needs a signal from outside, because intrinsic self-correction lowered accuracy in Huang's tests. So I name the criteria, cap the rounds, and keep the best-scoring draft. The gotcha is that the last draft isn't always the best.

Q · Mechanism — Why can a critique make things worse? A review prompt presumes there's something to fix, so the model tends to find something. It also shares the blind spots of the one that wrote the draft. With no outside signal, it has no new information. It's different if the input carries a failed test or a label, because that's new evidence. Agentic reflection owns where such feedback must come from.

Q · Trade-off — Loop, or one call with a verify line? One call with a verify line is the simpler rung: Anthropic documents "Before you finish, verify your answer against [test criteria]". I'd use it first, and on Opus 5 I'd leave it out, since that guide warns of over-verifying. A loop earns its calls when I need to inspect or score the intermediate draft, or a checker can feed it. For reasoning with no checker, I'd sample and vote.

Compare

Variant Signal Scope Use when
Self-refine model's own critique one output subjective, multi-criteria
Feedback-driven repair validator or test one output a check exists (repair loops)
Reflexion outcome per attempt across attempts retries with memory

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Gain where criteria are rich 25.4 → 74.6% dialogue task, GPT-4, 2023 cited (paper): Madaan et al.
Gain on maths 92.9 → 93.1% GPT-4, 2023 cited (paper): Madaan et al.
Self-correct, GSM8K 95.5 → 91.5 → 89.0% GPT-4, 200 samples, intrinsic cited (paper): Huang et al.

Pitfalls

  • "More rounds keep improving it"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the first round usually helps a lot, and the loop is one line to extend.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the paper caps at four rounds, and each one costs full calls, with no promise that a score keeps rising.
    ↳ Think instead: find the round where the mean stops rising on your set.
  • "Asking it to check its work can't hurt"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a human reviewer rarely makes a correct answer worse, and it reads as diligence.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: with no outside signal, a critique prompt presumes a flaw. GPT-4 fell on GSM8K in Huang's run.
    ↳ Think instead: give the critic new evidence, or skip it.
  • Not the same: self-refine vs a repair loop
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "generate, check, try again" in a loop.
    ↳ Difference: repair has a validator's verdict, which is ground truth for shape. Self-refine has the model's opinion.
    ↳ Think instead: if code can check it, use repair.
  • Don't reach for a loop before a better single prompt.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a loop looks like a quality guarantee and it's easy to bolt on.
    ↳ What goes wrong: cost multiplies and latency is serial, for what a better instruction may fix.
    ↳ Do instead: try the simpler rung: named criteria and a verify line in the first prompt.
  • Shelf life: in-call thinking will take the easy cases. A critique's need for a source of truth is durable.

Connections

Path:prompt chainingself-refineReflexionagentic reflection
  • Builds on prompt chaining: a chain that goes around again.
  • Owned elsewhere: agentic reflection owns where feedback must come from; repair loops own validator-driven retries.
  • Contrasts with self-consistency: parallel samples against serial rewrites.
  • Depends on LLM-as-judge: when the score is a model's.

notes.title: Reflexion — A Written Lesson Carried to the Next Attempt
notes.html:
References

Shinn et al. 2023: Reflexion

TL;DR

After a failed attempt, the model writes why it failed; that note goes into the context of the next attempt. Lessons cross attempts as text, with nothing changing in the weights. The agent loop is owned by Reflexion and self-critique; this is a pointer.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request

Recall

Prompt Answer
vs self-refine Self-refine revises one output; Reflexion carries lessons across attempts.
Prerequisite A real outcome per attempt: tests, a reward or a checkable goal.
Why "verbal" Feedback is text in the context, not a weight update.

The idea

Self-refine works on one draft and depends on the model's own opinion. Reflexion needs a verdict from outside, so its note can name what really failed. On HumanEval Python it took GPT-4 from 80.1% to 91%, but on MBPP Python it fell from 80.1% to 77.1%, so the gain isn't general. It also reported gains of 22% on AlfWorld and 20% on HotPotQA.

The prompting part is one instruction: "Given this failure, state what to do differently." It's a request. Reflections are model text, so treat them as untrusted when they persist.

Evolution

Lineage:Mar 2023 Self-RefineMar 2023 Reflexion2024 onward agent memory holds such lessons. 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): the pattern lives on in agent loops, as agentic reflection.

notes.title: Reasoning Models — How the Prompt Changes When the Model Thinks by Itself
notes.html:
References

OpenAI: reasoning best practices · Anthropic: prompting best practices · Snell et al. 2024: test-time compute · DeepSeek-R1 2025

TL;DR

A reasoning model produces its own working before it answers, because it was trained on outcomes, not because a prompt asked. So the prompt gets shorter: the step-by-step lines come out, the goal and the checks stay, and how hard it thinks moves into a setting. Old scaffolds can now cost you, up to a refusal. This note owns the edit to the prompt.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:old CoT promptdelete trigger and step liststate goal and success checktagged or schema answerset effort in the requesteval against the old prompt

Recall

Prompt Answer
What comes out of the prompt? Trigger sentences, prescribed steps, requests for a visible scratchpad.
What stays in the prompt? The goal, constraints, output contract, and a check it can run.
What replaces "think harder"? A request setting: effort or thinking level, read from the Landscape.

The idea

You move a working CoT prompt unchanged: "Think step by step. Step 1, list the figures. Step 2, compute the net. Show your reasoning in <thinking> tags." Here the model plans anyway, so your steps constrain it and the output grows. On some current Claude models a request like that is declined outright, and the refusal is billed if it comes before any output (Anthropic, as of Sep 2026).

The change is a deletion. State what a correct result is and how to check it, then leave the route to the model. Vendors now say this directly: OpenAI calls "think step by step" unnecessary here; Anthropic says to prefer general instructions over prescriptive steps. How much it reasons is a request parameter, handled in thinking controls.

The goal text is a request, and the setting is advisory. What's enforced is the output cap and the extractor.

The trade: you give up the control that scripted steps seemed to offer and pay for reasoning you often can't read, for better results on hard tasks and a shorter prompt.

How it works

The engineered prompt, shorter than the one it replaces.

① ROLE         You check invoices for a finance team.                     ← one line
② TASK         Work out the amount owed.                                  ← the goal, no route
③ CONSTRAINTS  Use only the figures given. If one is missing, say which.  ← a way out
④ CONTEXT      <invoice>{{invoice_text}}</invoice>                        ← arrived text: data
⑤ OUTPUT       Before finishing, verify the sum. Give the figure in <answer> tags. ← the check, the tag
Rule What actually happens
Trained on outcomes Rewards reach back through the reasoning, so the model learned to reason, not to imitate worked text.
Verification is a good ask Anthropic suggests asking for a check against test criteria. Opus 5 can over-verify, so its guide removes it.
Sampling knobs may go Claude 4.7+ rejects temperature; OpenAI says to remove it when effort is set.
Effort isn't the first fix OpenAI: effort is "not the primary way to recover quality". Fix the prompt, then raise it.

Evolution

Lineage:Aug 2024 test-time compute measuredSep 2024 o1 hides the chainJan 2025 DeepSeek-R1, open weights and visible reasoning2025 hybrid models with a thinking setting2026 thinking on by default, some models always on
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): the default for hard work, while controls change model by model.
  • Stronger-model test: yes for the scaffolds, which is the point of this note. What won't change: you state the goal and the check.
  • Checked on: vendor guides read 31 Oct 2026, for GPT-6 and GPT-5.x families and for Claude 5 and 4.x families. Snell's figures are for a fine-tuned PaLM 2-S* on MATH.

Code

The migration, as a diff.

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) Think step by step. Step 1… Step 2… Show your reasoning in <thinking> tags. Work out the amount owed. Before finishing, verify the sum.
On the input the same invoice more output, a billed refusal on some models a tagged figure, thinking handled by the model
Fails as steps fight the model's plan; a visible reasoning request is refused —
The one edit — ② and ⑤: deleting the route and keeping the goal and the check

Measure it

  • Offline: the old prompt against the shortened one at two or three effort settings, on a golden set, comparing accuracy per thousand tokens.
  • In production: thinking tokens per request, refusals by category, incomplete replies, and time to first answer token.
  • Enforced by: the output cap and the extractor. The effort setting and the verification line are guidance only.

Interview

30-second answer: A reasoning model does its own working, so I take the step-by-step lines out of the prompt, keep the goal, constraints, output contract and a success check, and set effort in the request. Hard work gets better, at the price of hidden billed reasoning. The gotcha is that an old scaffold isn't harmless: asking for a visible scratchpad can be refused on some current models.

Q · Mechanism — Why is a reasoning model different from CoT, if both produce steps? CoT is a chat model imitating worked solutions that it sees in the prompt or in training data. A reasoning model is trained on outcomes, with the training and serving side owned in LLM-Production. So the prompt's job moves from showing how to reason to saying what success is. Vendors also keep the chain out of reach, so what you read is a summary.

Q · Trade-off — When do I still use a smaller, non-reasoning route? The simpler rung is a fast model with a plain prompt, and I'd keep it wherever the eval shows no gain: extraction, classification, short rewrites. Reasoning tokens are output tokens, so that traffic would pay for nothing. Prompted CoT remains only for a model with thinking off. I'd check by slice, with routing by difficulty.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Efficiency over best-of-N up to 4× less compute PaLM 2-S*, MATH, 64 vs 256 samples, 2024 cited (paper): Snell et al.
Compute instead of model size beats ~14× larger model where the base model has non-trivial success cited (paper): Snell et al.

Pitfalls

  • "Keep the old CoT prompt: it can't hurt"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it passed its eval, and removing working text feels like removing safety.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: prescribed steps can narrow what the model would have done, and visible scratchpads can be refused on some Claude models.
    ↳ Think instead: re-run the eval with the scaffold deleted.
  • Not the same: effort vs model tier
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "spend more for a better answer" dials, and both change the bill.
    ↳ Difference: tier chooses the model and its price per token. Effort tells that model how much to spend on one request.
    ↳ Think instead: pick the tier by evals across traffic, and effort per task class.
  • Don't expose hidden reasoning to get debuggable prompts.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: you can't fix what you can't see, and old chains were readable.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the raw chain isn't returned by these APIs, and attempting extraction triggers refusals.
    ↳ Do instead: use summaries, and add a short explanation field. Don't name it reasoning.
  • Don't move every route to a reasoning model.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one model and one prompt is simpler, and it scores best on hard cases.
    ↳ What goes wrong: easy traffic pays for thinking it doesn't need and waits longer.
    ↳ Do instead: start with the simpler rung, and add thinking where a slice's eval needs it.
  • Shelf life: the parameter names change quarterly. Goal and check in the prompt, depth in a setting, is the durable part.

Connections

Path:when CoT hurtsreasoning modelsthinking controlsmodel-upgrade migration
  • Supersedes chain-of-thought: the prompted form becomes a fallback.
  • Owned elsewhere: reasoning models and test-time compute owns training and serving; reasoning models as agents owns the agent side.
  • Used by model-upgrade migration: deleting scaffolds is a migration step.
  • Differs by model: model-family differences.
  • Drilled in reasoning model or prompted CoT.

notes.title: When Chain-of-Thought Hurts — Narrow Gains, Real Costs, False Explanations
notes.html:
References

Sprague et al. 2024: To CoT or not to CoT? · Turpin et al. 2023: unfaithful explanations · Anthropic: handling refusals

TL;DR

Across 110 papers, chain-of-thought gains concentrate on symbolic, maths and logic tasks; everything else averages under a point. The cost doesn't shrink with the gain: output tokens and waiting time are paid on every request that carries the instruction. And the chain isn't a record of why the model answered: a hint in the prompt can move the answer without appearing in the steps.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:requestdoes the task need computing?direct promptcan a tool compute it?toolCoT with a captagged answerchain kept as debug text only

Recall

Prompt Answer
Where are gains near zero? Outside symbolic, maths and logic: 56.8 against 56.1 on average.
What beat CoT where it helps? Writing a plan, then running it in a real solver.
What is unfaithful reasoning? Stated steps omit what really moved the answer, such as a suggested option.

The idea

A team adds "think step by step" to a ticket classifier after a good demo. Accuracy doesn't move. Each reply grows from one label to a paragraph: spend rises, the answer arrives later, and the parser that read one word starts failing.

Then someone proposes showing the chain to agents as the reason for each label. That failure is worse. Turpin et al. added "I think the answer is (A)" to prompts: answers moved towards it, and the steps explained them on other grounds. The text reads as a trace and it is generated output.

Two separate questions, then: does this task gain (ask an eval, per slice), and can the chain be evidence (no).

Both limits are enforced only if you build them: a route that sends traffic to the simpler prompt, and an output that doesn't use the chain as a reason.

The trade: you keep CoT for the slice that earns it and give up the single prompt that handles everything, so you now run a route and two prompts.

How it works

1,218 comparisons across 110 papers.

Rule What actually happens
A mixed benchmark hides this Up to 95% of the CoT gain on MMLU came from questions containing "=". The overall number is a maths slice in disguise.
Latency is serial Reasoning tokens stream before the answer, so time to answer grows with the chain.
Cost scales with chain length Derived: a 10-token label plus 300 tokens of working is (300 + 10) / 10 = 31× the output tokens. Inputs illustrative.
A solver beats it on its own ground In Sprague's tests, planning with the model and executing in Python outperformed CoT for both steps.

Evolution

Lineage:May 2023 reasoning shown unfaithfulAug 2024 strict formats shown to remove the gainSep 2024 gains scoped across 110 papers2026 thinking moves out of the prompt; the costs move with it
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Oct 2026): the scope and the faithfulness results both stand, and hidden thinking only moves the bill.
  • Stronger-model test: partly. A task's gain can vanish on a stronger model; assume unfaithfulness holds. What won't change: output tokens are paid for and come before the answer.
  • Checked on: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 for Turpin; 14 models and 20 datasets for Sprague's own runs.

Code

The same classifier, before and after the route.

🔴 Naive 🟢 Engineered
Prompt (the part that differs) Think step by step, then give the label. Give the label only., and the CoT prompt kept for the slice that gains
On the input a routine ticket a paragraph and a label, no more accurate one label
Fails as flat accuracy, more tokens, parser misses —
The one edit — deleting the reasoning line for slices the eval shows don't gain

Measure it

  • Offline: per-slice accuracy of direct against CoT, with the slices weighted by live traffic. Keep CoT only where the gain survives that weighting.
  • In production: reasoning-to-answer token ratio per route, time to answer, parse-failure rate. The ratio rising on easy traffic shows a route leak.
  • Enforced by: routing code and the token cap, for where it runs and how long. That a chain reports true causes can't be enforced by anything.

Interview

30-second answer: CoT's gains concentrate on symbolic, maths and logic tasks: 110 papers show about 14, 12 and 7 points there and under one elsewhere. The cost is paid on every request, and even in that range a planner plus a real solver did better. So I route it by slice. The gotcha is faithfulness: the chain isn't a trace, so it never becomes the reason shown to a user.

Q · Mechanism — How can reasoning be unfaithful and still improve accuracy? Written steps improve accuracy by supplying intermediates later tokens read. Faithfulness says the text names what caused the answer. Turpin found a suggested answer in the prompt moved results, while 73% of the unfaithful explanations supported the bias-consistent answer without saying the hint had done it. The steps can compute something and still be silent about the cause.

Q · Trade-off — CoT helps your hardest 5% of traffic. Do you turn it on? For that slice, if I can route to it. The simpler rung is a single direct prompt, and it is right when I can't identify the slice cheaply, or when the gain on the slice is worth less than the cost on the other 95%. If it is feasible, direct is the default, CoT serves that slice, and I watch the route for leaks. If the slice is pure calculation, a tool replaces both.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Top-three tasks 45.5 → 56.9 mean, symbolic, maths, logic cited (paper): Sprague et al.
All other tasks 56.1 → 56.8 mean over the remaining categories cited (paper): Sprague et al.
Bias moves CoT accuracy −36.3 / −30.6% "Suggested Answer", zero-shot CoT, 13 BBH tasks, GPT-3.5 / Claude 1.0 cited (paper): Turpin et al.
Unfaithful chains 73% share supporting the bias-consistent answer cited (paper): Turpin et al.

Pitfalls

  • "Showing the reasoning makes the system transparent"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: users trust an answer with visible working, and the text looks like a log.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the chain is generated output. It can omit what moved the answer, so it adds confidence that nothing supports, which is worse than showing none.
    ↳ Think instead: show citations and rule ids that code can check.
  • "If CoT doesn't help, the worst case is a few wasted tokens"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: zero gain sounds like a neutral result, and one sentence looks harmless to leave in.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the task now has longer replies, later answers and a parser reading narration. Flat accuracy can come with new failures.
    ↳ Think instead: a change with no measured gain is a cost, so delete it.
  • Not the same: a benchmark gain vs a gain on your traffic
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: papers report one number, and the eval set is often weighted towards hard cases.
    ↳ Difference: a mixed set's gain can come from one slice. MMLU's mostly did. Your traffic has its own mix.
    ↳ Think instead: report the gain per slice, then weight the slices by live share.
  • Don't build a difficulty router before you've measured a slice.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: routing sounds like the architect's answer, and the two prompts already exist.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you run a classifier, two prompts and a leak monitor for a gain you haven't confirmed.
    ↳ Do instead: try the simpler rung: one prompt, one eval. Add a route once a slice shows a real gain.
  • Shelf life: which tasks gain will move with each model. The cost shape and the gap between useful and faithful are durable.

Connections

Path:chain-of-thoughtwhy it workswhen it hurtsrouting by difficulty
  • Builds on why CoT works: a mechanism with limits, measured here.
  • Depends on golden datasets: slices are what show a narrow gain.
  • Contrasts with compliance and auditability: what evidence looks like when a chain doesn't count.
  • Superseded by thinking controls: the same costs, in hidden tokens.
  • Owned elsewhere: output-format specification owns field order.

notes.title: Thinking Controls — Effort, Caps, and the Reply That Ran Out
notes.html:
References

Anthropic: thinking · Anthropic: effort · OpenAI: reasoning · Google: Gemini thinking

TL;DR

Depth of reasoning is now a request setting. All three providers steer it with a named level (effort or thinking level), and that level is guidance. Token budgets are on their way out. The hard limit is the output cap, and thinking and answer share it. Spend it on thinking and the reply stops with no answer, while you still pay. So the code that matters reads why the reply stopped. Each provider's names, levels and defaults are in the chapter map's Landscape.

Stage:decidewriteassemblecallshapeevaluateshipwatchevery request
Flow:set effortset output capmodel thinksmodel answersread stop reasoncount a failure, raise cap or lower effortlog thinking tokens

Recall

Prompt Answer
What is enforced: effort or cap? The cap. Effort is soft guidance to the model.
What does the cap cover? Thinking and visible answer together, on all three providers.
Is a cut-off reply billed? Yes. Tokens spent count, even with no visible output.

The idea

A pipeline sets a 2,000-token output cap, which was plenty for a one-paragraph JSON answer on the old model. After an upgrade, thinking is on by default. On a hard document the model thinks for 2,000 tokens and stops. The reply has no text, your parser reports a schema error, a retry repeats it, and the bill is the same as for a success.

"Set a thinking budget" no longer applies on the newest models: budget_tokens returns a 400 on Claude 4.7 and later, and Gemini's budget is deprecated on Gemini 4. Effort says how hard to try and bends to the task. The cap says when to stop, and doesn't bend.

The trade: you hand the model the choice of how much to think per request, which helps hard cases, and give up a predictable token count, so your code carries the cap, the check and the log.

How it works

Every provider reports why the reply stopped, under a different name.

Rule What actually happens
The cap is shared Derived: answer room = cap − thinking used. Cap 2,000, thinking 2,000: room 0.
Billing ignores what you can see Full thinking is billed as output, even when only a summary or nothing comes back.
Changing thinking breaks the cache On Anthropic, changing the thinking config or top-level effort invalidates cached prefixes.
Each tool-loop request has its own cap Thinking repeats per request, and prior-turn thinking can bill as input.
OpenAI's starting reserve Reserve at least 25,000 tokens in max_output_tokens when starting (Oct 2026).

Evolution

Lineage:Sep 2024 o1 hides the chainFeb 2025 token budgets on hybrid models2025 Gemini budgets, then levels2026 adaptive thinking, budgets deprecated, thinking on by defaultOct 2026 some Claude models can't turn it off
  • Maturity: 🟡 Maturing (Oct 2026): the shape has settled; names, levels and defaults still change per model.
  • Stronger-model test: no. A better model doesn't remove the cap, the bill or the branch. What won't change: reading the stop reason before the content.
  • Checked on: docs read 31 Oct 2026: Claude Fable, Mythos, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku families; GPT-5.x and GPT-6; Gemini 2.5 to 4. Re-check within 3 months.

Code

The control around the call, with Anthropic's field names and scripted responses.

def read(resp):
    u, stop = resp["usage"], resp["stop_reason"]
    thinking = u.get("output_tokens_details", {}).get("thinking_tokens", 0)
    log = {"thinking": thinking, "output": u["output_tokens"], "stop": stop}
    if stop in ("max_tokens", "refusal"):                 # failed, even if the text parses
        return None, log
    return "".join(b["text"] for b in resp["content"] if b["type"] == "text"), log

ok = {"stop_reason": "end_turn", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "4920"}],
      "usage": {"output_tokens": 348, "output_tokens_details": {"thinking_tokens": 312}}}
cut = {"stop_reason": "max_tokens", "content": [],
       "usage": {"output_tokens": 2000, "output_tokens_details": {"thinking_tokens": 2000}}}
print(read(ok)); print(read(cut))
# look for: cut returns None with thinking equal to the cap
# naive belief predicts: an empty reply means the model had nothing to say

Break it: the belief that a short reply is a short bill. Run on Python 3.15, it prints ('4920', {'thinking': 312, 'output': 348, 'stop': 'end_turn'}) then (None, {'thinking': 2000, 'output': 2000, 'stop': 'max_tokens'}). The second cost 2,000 output tokens and returned nothing.

Measure it

  • Offline: two or three effort levels on a golden set, by accuracy and by p95 thinking tokens. Set the cap from that p95 plus the answer's size, and add headroom.
  • In production: thinking tokens per route, rate of cap stops, refusals, retries on cap stops. A rising cap-stop rate after an upgrade is the alarm.
  • Enforced by: the output cap and your stop-reason branch. Effort and any prompt steering are guidance only.

Interview

30-second answer: I set effort per task class and an output cap that covers thinking plus the answer, because they share it. Effort is soft guidance; only the cap is enforced. Then I read the stop reason before the content. The gotcha is that a reply cut off in thinking looks like an empty or invalid output, and it's billed anyway, so a blind retry pays twice.

Q · Mechanism — Effort or budget: what changed? A budget asked for a token target; it was a target, not a cap, and it fitted one number to very different requests. Effort names an intent, and the model decides per request. On Anthropic, budget_tokens is deprecated on Opus and Sonnet 4.6 and returns a 400 on Claude 4.7 and later. Gemini 4 maps a lone budget to the nearest level with a warning. So budget code needs migrating.

Q · Trade-off — Should I raise effort or fix the prompt? Fix the prompt first. The simpler rung is default effort with clearer instructions and a success check, and OpenAI's guide says effort is "not the primary way to recover quality". I raise it only when the eval shows that a slice gains and the cost holds. Lowering it is often the better change: if traffic is easy, cost and latency improve together.

Compare

What you want Anthropic OpenAI Google
Stop signal stop_reason: "max_tokens" status: "incomplete" "incomplete" status
Depth control output_config.effort reasoning.effort thinking_level
Hard cap max_tokens max_output_tokens max_output_tokens
Thinking count thinking_tokens reasoning_tokens total_thought_tokens

Pitfalls

  • "Higher effort means a better answer"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's named like a quality dial, and the top level sounds safest.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it buys more thinking, which helps only tasks that need it. OpenAI says effort isn't the primary way to recover quality.
    ↳ Think instead: sweep it on an eval and keep the lowest level that passes.
  • "A low cap saves money"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a cap looks like a spending limit, and it's the one enforced number.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a stop at the cap pays for all of those tokens and returns no answer, then the retry pays again. Google's guide says to lower the level instead.
    ↳ Think instead: control spend with effort; set the cap as a ceiling on runaway replies.
  • Not the same: thinking summary vs thinking
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the summary arrives in a thinking block, so it looks like the reasoning.
    ↳ Difference: a summary is a condensed version, and billing follows the full chain. Claude 5 defaults to omitted, so nothing may appear.
    ↳ Think instead: read the token count for cost, and a summary only for a rough debugging view.
  • Don't build an effort classifier before a fixed level fails.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: per-request tuning sounds efficient, and thinking is a large cost line.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a classifier is a new model to evaluate, while adaptive thinking already varies depth by request.
    ↳ Do instead: try the simpler rung, one level per route, and change it after an eval.
  • Shelf life: parameter names and defaults here last months, so re-check every 3 months. Sharing the cap and reading the stop reason are the durable ideas.

Connections

Path:reasoning modelsthinking controlscost modelingobservability
  • Builds on reasoning models: what to delete from the prompt first.
  • Used by reliability engineering: cap stops are a failure class to count.
  • Depends on output length control: the same cap, seen from the visible side.
  • Contrasts with deterministic prompting: temperature is rejected on some models that think.
  • Differs by model: model-family differences.
  • Drilled in reasoning model or prompted CoT.
